# OS command built from HTTP request data (Python)

`qualor:python/command-injection` · Issue · Severity: High · [CWE-78](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/78.html) · OWASP Top 10: [A05:2025 Injection](https://top10.owasp.org/2025/A05_2025-Injection/), [A03:2021 Injection](https://top10.owasp.org/2021/A03_2021-Injection/)

## What it finds

<!-- begin: what-it-finds -->
HTTP request data in a Flask, Django or FastAPI application that reaches an operating system
command:

- a command string that a shell runs: `os.system()`, `os.popen()`, `subprocess.getoutput()` and
  `getstatusoutput()`, the `subprocess` functions (`run`, `call`, `check_call`, `check_output`,
  `Popen`) with `shell=True`, `asyncio.create_subprocess_shell()` and `loop.subprocess_shell()`;
- the command of a shell program in an argument list: the element after `sh -c` (or `bash`,
  `zsh`, ...), and every element after `cmd /c` or `powershell -Command`;
- the program itself: the first element of an argument list, a program string without a shell,
  `executable=`, the program of `asyncio.create_subprocess_exec()`, or a whole argument list sent
  by the client (`request.args.getlist("argv")`, `shlex.split(request.form["cmd"])`).

A fixed program with request data only as further list elements is not reported, also when the
list is a fixed command line split into words (`f"ping -c 1 {host}".split()`): without a shell,
each element reaches the program as one argument.
<!-- end: what-it-finds -->

## Why it matters

<!-- begin: why-it-matters -->
A shell reads metacharacters such as `;`, `|`, `&&` and `$(...)` in the command text, so a
client who controls part of it can run any other command with the rights of the server. When the
client picks the program, it runs whatever program it names, with the arguments the code adds.
<!-- end: why-it-matters -->

## Example

<!-- begin: example -->
**Noncompliant:** the host name from the query string is pasted into a shell command.

```python
import subprocess

from flask import Flask, request

app = Flask(__name__)


@app.route("/ping")
def ping():
    host = request.args["host"]
    out = subprocess.run("ping -c 1 " + host, shell=True, capture_output=True)
    return out.stdout
```

**Compliant:** a fixed program with an argument list and no shell; the host name is one argument.

```python
import subprocess

from flask import Flask, request

app = Flask(__name__)


@app.route("/ping")
def ping():
    host = request.args["host"]
    out = subprocess.run(["ping", "-c", "1", "--", host], capture_output=True)
    return out.stdout
```
<!-- end: example -->

## How to fix

<!-- begin: how-to-fix -->
- Run a fixed program with an argument list and without a shell:
  `subprocess.run(["git", "log", ref])`, `asyncio.create_subprocess_exec("git", "log", ref)`.
- To let users choose a program or an action, look it up in a fixed allow-list (a module-level
  dict of constants, whose values may be argument lists).
- If a shell is unavoidable, quote each value with `shlex.quote()` (or build the line with
  `shlex.join()`). It escapes for POSIX shells only, not for `cmd.exe` or PowerShell.
- Convert numbers with `int()` or `float()`.
<!-- end: how-to-fix -->

## Frameworks and APIs covered

- Flask
- Django
- FastAPI
- `subprocess`
- `asyncio`

## Known limits

<!-- begin: known-limits -->
- An allow-list check before the call (`if tool not in ("uptime", "df"): return`) is not
  recognised; a lookup in a module-level dict of constants is.
- A slice is followed when it slices request data in place (`request.args["cmd"][:100]`),
  a variable assigned request data, or a view parameter; a slice of a value built from request
  data (`(request.args["q"] + "x")[:50]`) is missed.
- With `shell=True`, only the first element of an argument list is taken for shell code, as on
  POSIX; on Windows the other elements reach `cmd.exe` too. `shlex.quote()` is accepted as
  escaping also in a `cmd /c` command.
- A shell program's command is followed when its argument list is written in the call or assigned
  to a variable just before it; a POSIX shell's `-c` counts after up to three option words, and
  PowerShell's shortened parameter names (`-Comm`, `-enc`) are not recognised.
- Without a shell, a program is recognised when it is visibly a string, a request value, a view
  parameter or a variable assigned one of these; a program concatenated from names only
  (`TOOL_DIR + tool`) is missed. A variable that held request data and then a list with a fixed
  program, and a helper's list passed with `shell=True`, are reported.
- `os.exec*()` and `os.spawn*()` are not covered.
- Request sources are recognised by their shape. A Flask route parameter with a converter
  (`<int:n>`) and a Django URL argument made numeric by its converter still count as request data;
  a function whose first parameter is named `request`, in a module that imports Django, is taken
  for a view; a Flask view parameter annotated `int` is not a source.
<!-- end: known-limits -->

## Tests

The test file [`rules/python/command/command-injection.py`](../../../rules/python/command/command-injection.py) holds every case the rule reports or accepts:
lines marked `ruleid:` must be reported and lines marked `ok:` must not. The known limits are
marked `todoruleid:` (missed) and `todook:` (wrongly reported). `npm test` runs them with OpenGrep,
and checks the example above as well.
